clue.text: Beheaded his mother in Holland — little beast!

definitions.text: Beheaded his mother in Holland — little beast!

parts.words: Beheaded his mother in Holland — little beast!
parts.note: the small pet's dam, written together, loses its first letter and becomes the Dutch capital

explanation.surface: A shocking report of a killing in the Netherlands by a small brute.
explanation.walkthrough: Write the pet plus DAM (a mother animal) and drop the first letter: you get AMSTERDAM, a city in Holland.
explanation.definitionFit: This small rodent kept as a pet is a little beast.

clue.text: Married a song-writer at Battle River

parts.note: Thomas Arne composed Rule, Britannia!

explanation.surface: A wedding where a composer performs, held at a riverside battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Arne was the 18th-century English composer of Rule, Britannia!
explanation.definitionFit: This French river gave its name to battles in both world wars.

clue.text: Biggest noise in Fleet Street

parts.note: Fleet Street was the home of London newspapers, and the most famous of them had a booming nickname

explanation.surface: The loudest voice among London's newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street is the London street once home to the national press; The Times was nicknamed for its thundering editorials.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the nickname of The Times newspaper, known for booming editorials.

clue.text: One in blue goes up to the platform

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means the letters are read from bottom to top
in places the numeral inside the word for blue

parts.note: blue means sad or low
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone feeling low climbs onto a stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts I inside SAD to make SIAD, and 'goes up' reverses that.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised stage at the end of a hall is a platform.

clue.text: Cheeky monkey is after money in the trading centre

indicators.note: in places the money and monkey inside the market

parts.note: a mart is a market

indicators.note: after places the monkey behind the money

parts.note: L is the pound sign, so money
an ape is a monkey

explanation.surface: A naughty monkey follows the cash around a marketplace.
explanation.definitionFit: This old word means impudent or saucy, the same as cheeky.

clue.text: Scandinavian giant fish

explanation.surface: A huge Norse figure goes angling.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb 'fish' means to trail a line behind a boat, which is the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In Norse folklore it is a giant or ogre; as a verb it means trailing a baited line.

clue.text: Bind broken lamp — brought in a bit of money

indicators.note: brought in means the jumbled letters are taken inside the money word

parts.note: a coin is a single piece of money

indicators.note: broken means the letters of lamp are rearranged

explanation.surface: Fix a broken lamp, earning a little cash for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' scrambles the lamp and 'brought in' puts it inside the money. 'Bind' looks like tie, but here it is British slang for moan.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a bind is a nuisance, and to bind is to grumble or moan.

clue.text: Commercial outlet before Christmas

parts.note: an ad is a commercial
a vent is an outlet for air

explanation.surface: Seasonal advertising pours out in the run-up to the holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase standing for the church season of the four weeks preceding the feast.
explanation.definitionFit: The church season of the four weeks preceding the Nativity feast bears this name.

clue.text: … but what sort of creature is reassembled contrariwise by a wall?

annotationWithheld.why: … but what sort of creature is reassembled contrariwise by a wall? (9): no parse found that builds the letters from 'reassembled contrariwise by a wall'; the clue runs on from 1 across, whose wordplay is also unresolved
annotationWithheld.clue: … but what sort of creature is reassembled contrariwise by a wall?

clue.text: Like I ac Latin poet receives nothing

indicators.note: the poet takes something into himself, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Ovid was the Roman poet of the Metamorphoses
O looks like a zero, meaning nothing

explanation.surface: A comparison with a Roman versifier who is handed nothing for his trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I ac' is the OCR of '1 ac', meaning 1 across: the egg-shaped character who sat on a wall. 'receives' puts O inside OVID.
explanation.definitionFit: The character at 1 across is an egg, and something egg-shaped is described with this adjective.

clue.text: With it seek to assimilate the latest thing

indicators.note: to assimilate is to take in and absorb, so one word swallows the other

parts.note: to seek is to try or attempt
the latest part of anything is its end

explanation.surface: Advice to absorb whatever fashion has just arrived if you want to keep up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With it' looks like a linking phrase but is the definition, in its 1960s slang sense of fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Being with it is slang for being fashionable and up to date.

clue.text: But this order's wrong for one going to bed

definitions.text: But this order's wrong for one going to bed

parts.words: But this order's wrong for one going to bed
parts.note: a phrase meaning perfect neatness is also the name of a schoolboy prank where the sheets are folded so the sleeper cannot stretch out

explanation.surface: A neat arrangement of bedding that turns out to be a trick on whoever climbs in.
explanation.walkthrough: The same food word makes two idioms: one 'order' means perfectly tidy, while the 'bed' version is a British boarding-school prank of folding the sheet back on itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both immaculate tidiness and a practical joke made with folded sheets.

clue.text: Notice about foreign currency

parts.note: re means concerning or about
the mark was the German unit of money

explanation.surface: An announcement about exchange rates for overseas money.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice something is to observe it, and to comment on it is likewise to observe aloud.

clue.text: Seeing me quietly strike one, start to cry "Foul!"'

parts.note: taken as written
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, quietly
to hit is to strike
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: start to signals the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone watches me hit a player quietly and starts shouting foul.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'quietly', OCR'd as 'quickly'; P for piano means softly in music.
explanation.definitionFit: This rare adjective describes a noxious, foul-smelling vapour.

clue.text: Thraso was one entitled to bestride artillery horse

indicators.note: to bestride is to straddle, so the outer word sits astride the others

parts.note: a baronet holds a title, abbreviated Bart
RA is the Royal Artillery
gee-gee is a child's word for a horse, shortened to GG

explanation.surface: A titled man sits astride a gun-team horse, much as a vain soldier might.
explanation.walkthrough: Thraso is the boastful soldier in Terence's comedy The Eunuch, the classic type of the bragging warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: Thraso is the stock boastful soldier of Roman comedy, a type of the loud boaster.

clue.text: Giant could have given Agag a turn

indicators.note: could have given suggests the letters might be rearranged to give something new

explanation.surface: A giant might have made the biblical king Agag spin round.
explanation.walkthrough: Agag was an Amalekite king in the Bible; 'turn' is fodder, not the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabelais's character is a huge, gluttonous giant.

clue.text: Shoots a lot of cattle, basis for ostracism

parts.note: to pot is to shoot game
a herd is a large group of cattle

explanation.surface: A gunman shoots a herd of cows.
explanation.walkthrough: In ancient Athens votes to banish a citizen were scratched on broken pottery, giving the word ostracism.
explanation.definitionFit: Athenians wrote names on broken pottery fragments to vote for banishment.

clue.text: Hire pony, potential Derby winner…

indicators.note: something potential is not yet formed, so these letters are still to be arranged into the horse

parts.note: the fodder, nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone hires a pony in the hope it may win England's greatest flat race.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is the premier English flat race at Epsom; the 1933 winner bore this name, also that of a Titan, which links on to 19 across.
explanation.definitionFit: This colt won the Epsom Derby in 1933, so it is a specific winner of that race.

clue.text: Young locust found in a Kentish garden?

explanation.surface: An immature insect turns up in a garden in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent, a county in south-east England, is famous for hop gardens, where hop pickers worked.
explanation.definitionFit: An immature locust is called this; so is a picker working the hop fields.

clue.text: … whose sire, we hear, you ran to America to find

indicators.note: we hear signals that the words are judged by their sound when spoken

parts.note: spoken, these two words give the start of the planet's name
US is the United States

explanation.surface: Someone sprints off to the States in search of a forefather.
explanation.walkthrough: Runs on from 18 across: in Greek myth the Titan of that name was a son of the sky god, so 'whose sire' points to the father.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the sky god fathered the Titans, including the one named at 18 across.

clue.text: One testing evidence of Sister Susie's skill

explanation.surface: A tester inspects Sister Susie's needlework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sister Susie's Sewing Shirts for Soldiers' is a First World War song; an embroidered sampler shows needle skill.
explanation.definitionFit: One who tests is a taster; an embroidered piece showing stitches displays needle skill.

clue.text: Royalty incorporated in one of the media

indicators.note: in signals the abbreviation is placed inside the media word

parts.note: the press is newspapers, one of the mass media

explanation.surface: A royal figure becomes a company director in newspaper publishing.
explanation.definitionFit: A king's daughter is a member of the royal family, so she counts as royalty.

clue.text: A catch in this for the Indian student

parts.note: the Cree are a Native American people
L is a learner, so a student

explanation.surface: Fish caught for a Native American learner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian' means North American Indian here; L is the learner plate on British cars.
explanation.definitionFit: An angler's wicker basket holds the day's fish.

clue.text: Type of wood. Many get resin from it

parts.note: balsa is a very light tropical timber
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so many

explanation.surface: A note that people extract a sticky resin from a certain tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The full stop splits the clue: the wood and 'Many' build the answer, 'get' joins them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an aromatic resinous substance exuded by certain trees.

clue.text: Direction to get stuff and push off

parts.note: S is south, a compass direction
to cram is to stuff

explanation.surface: An order to gather belongings and leave.
explanation.definitionFit: This slang imperative means go away, leave at once.

clue.text: Bound to come together, it's said

indicators.note: it's said signals that the words are judged as spoken

parts.note: to meet is to come together

explanation.surface: A promise to meet up.
explanation.definitionFit: As an old noun it means a boundary or limit.

clue.text: Oriental topper rejected by the best people

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the pair of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: E is short for eastern or oriental
tile is old slang for a hat, something worn on top

explanation.surface: Fashionable society turns its nose up at an Eastern hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns E plus TILE together, giving the run backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The cream of society, the select few, are its chosen group.

clue.text: Choose to take an exam for this college?

parts.note: to elect is to choose by vote
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A student picks an exam to get into a particular college.
explanation.walkthrough: The college is the American body that formally chooses the president, not an academic one.
explanation.definitionFit: The American body of delegates choosing a president is called by this adjective plus college.

clue.text: Smith's contribution to the Nutcracker Suite — percussion section?

definitions.text: Smith's contribution to the Nutcracker Suite — percussion section?

parts.words: Smith's contribution to the Nutcracker Suite — percussion section?
parts.note: a blacksmith's heavy tool would be a crude nutcracker, and it could pass as a loud instrument in an orchestra

explanation.surface: A man named Smith adds a part to Tchaikovsky's ballet music for the drums.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smith' is not a composer but a blacksmith, whose big striking tool would crack nuts brutally.
explanation.definitionFit: A blacksmith's heavy long-handled striking tool would crush nuts and beat like a drum.
